stem: Patrick is a 6-month-old infant with severe bronchiolitis: marked chest wall retractions, grunting, pallor, respiratory rate 80/min, heart rate 190/min, and oxygen saturation 80% on room air. Which is the most appropriate sequence of respiratory support to trial as his condition worsens, from least to most invasive?

options.text: Low-flow nasal prongs → blow-over mask oxygen → high-flow humidified oxygen → nasopharyngeal CPAP → intubation and ventilation
Blow-over mask oxygen → low-flow nasal prongs → high-flow humidified oxygen → nasopharyngeal CPAP → intubation and ventilation
Low-flow nasal prongs → high-flow humidified oxygen → nasopharyngeal CPAP → intubation and ventilation → blow-over mask oxygen
Blow-over mask oxygen → high-flow humidified oxygen → low-flow nasal prongs → nasopharyngeal CPAP → intubation and ventilation
High-flow humidified oxygen → nasopharyngeal CPAP → intubation and ventilation → low-flow nasal prongs → blow-over mask oxygen

explanation: In an infant with severe bronchiolitis and hypoxaemic respiratory distress, escalation is from simple oxygen delivery to more advanced respiratory support: humidified high-flow oxygen, then CPAP, and finally intubation and ventilation if the child deteriorates or fails non-invasive support.

citations.title: Practice Quiz: Emergency Medicine - Breathing difficulties

rationale: The source item was an ordering question, so it was rewritten as a single-best-answer question asking for the correct escalation sequence.

optionExplanations.A: This is not a sensible escalation sequence: blow-over oxygen is simpler than nasal prongs, and high-flow should come before CPAP and ventilation.
optionExplanations.B: Low-flow nasal prongs are not usually preferred over blow-over oxygen as the first simple oxygen strategy in this context, and the sequence is otherwise out of order.
optionExplanations.C: Ventilation is far more invasive than the other modalities and would not precede them in an escalation pathway.
optionExplanations.D: Low-flow nasal prongs should not come after high-flow oxygen in an escalation sequence.
optionExplanations.E: This is the best sequence: escalate from high-flow humidified oxygen to CPAP, then to intubation and ventilation if required.

Instructions

The following nine questions refer to Patrick’s clinical scenario.

Clinical scenario 1 - Patrick

Patrick, a six month old infant, is brought to the emergency department with wheezing and respiratory distress. On examination he has severe chest wall retractions, grunting and is pale. His vital signs are:

RR 80/min, HR 190/min, temperature 38.0’C, SaO2 80% in room air.

The accompanying table has the normal ranges indicated in the 2010 NSW Health Standard Paediatric Observation Chart, SPOC.

Patrick has wheeze and crackles throughout his chest. There is a history of having been snuffly with a cough for the last two days. The entire family has a cold.

answerRecovery.notes: Blow-over oxygen is included as a distractor to reflect the source wording, but clinically high-flow humidified oxygen is the relevant escalation step before CPAP in severe bronchiolitis.
